title: From Naissus to New Rome: the Hostage, the Sign, and the City That Took His Name
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Hostage at the Eastern Court

stops.name: Naissus, the birth in the garrison town
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the year is given variously as 272 and 273, and 27 February comes from later commemorative calendars rather than from any contemporary record
stops.campa: Flavius Valerius Constantinus is born at Naissus in Moesia Superior, a road town on the Danube approaches where the legions are quartered and the emperors keep passing through. His father Constantius, called Chlorus, is a Balkan officer on the rise. His mother Helena is a woman of no recorded family, and the sources cannot agree whether she is Constantius's wife or his concubine; they do not settle it. Nothing in the town marks the birth. He will build a villa in the suburb of Mediana when he is emperor, sixty years on, and that is the only monument Naissus gets.
suggested_refs: The imperial villa at Mediana outside Nis, built by Constantine himself and not standing at the date of his birth

stops.name: Nicomedia, the boy at the court of Diocletian
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: his arrival at the eastern court is placed around 293, when the tetrarchy is formed and his father is raised to caesar; no source dates it exactly
stops.campa: Constantius is made caesar of the West and sets Helena aside to marry Theodora, stepdaughter of the augustus Maximian. His son by Helena is sent east to Diocletian at Nicomedia, honored as a young officer and held as a pledge: while the boy is at court, the father in Gaul stays loyal. Constantine grows up in the largest palace in the empire, learning Greek, watching four emperors run a system built by a man who believes succession can be engineered. He is being taught, without anyone intending it, exactly how a tetrarchy comes apart.
suggested_refs: The tetrarchic palace quarter at Nicomedia, Diocletian's eastern capital

stops.name: Antioch, tribune of the first order
stops.date_confidence: attested as service, unfixed in detail: the Persian war runs from 297 to 299 and the Origo places Constantine in it, but no source tracks his rank and movements year by year
stops.campa: The Persian war is staged out of Antioch and Constantine rides in it as a tribune. The command is Galerius's, not Diocletian's; the senior augustus is in Egypt that season putting down the usurper Domitius Domitianus. Galerius is beaten badly in Mesopotamia, then comes back and destroys Narseh, and the peace of Nisibis hands Rome five provinces beyond the Tigris. Constantine sees at first hand what a Balkan soldier of no family can take out of an eastern empire, and how fast one defeat can be turned over.
suggested_refs: The Peace of Nisibis, 299, high-water mark of Roman power east of the Tigris

stops.name: Nicomedia, the church pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested: Lactantius dates the demolition to 23 February 303 and the posting of the first edict to the following day; the two are often conflated
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of February the prefect's men go to the church that stands in full view of the palace at Nicomedia, force the doors, burn the scriptures, and level the building before evening. The next morning the first edict of the persecution is posted: churches razed, books surrendered, Christians stripped of rank and of standing at law. Constantine is thirty and he is at court. Eusebius will later place him at Diocletian's side through all of it. Nothing he does for the next nine years suggests he objected out loud.
suggested_refs: The Diocletianic edict of 24 February 303, first of four against the Christians

stops.name: Gesoriacum, the crossing to his father
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline, legendary in detail: the flight is recorded by the Origo and the panegyrists, who supply the hamstrung post horses
stops.campa: Diocletian and Maximian abdicate together and the new tetrarchy passes over Constantine entirely. Galerius keeps him at court, then lets him go, or he simply goes. The panegyrists have him riding out at night and crippling the post horses behind him at every station so that the recall order can never catch up. He reaches Gesoriacum on the Channel coast and crosses to his father, who is already in Britain. Constantius has one campaigning season left in him and does not know it.
suggested_refs: The Roman Channel port of Gesoriacum, the crossing point of the British command

stops.name: Beyond Hadrian's Wall, the Pictish campaign
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, approximate in place and date: the campaign is normally set in the summer of 306, no source names the ground it was fought on, and the pin stands at the Wall itself
stops.campa: Father and son go north past the Wall against the Picts, the last campaign of Constantius's life and the first Constantine fights at his side rather than under strangers. They win, or they are said to win; the panegyric that reports it cares more about the weather and the son's presence than about the fighting. What matters is who is watching. The army of Britain, the guard, the Alamannic auxiliaries: an entire field force sees the old augustus dying and the young man riding next to him.
suggested_refs: Hadrian's Wall and the northern frontier command inherited by Constantine in 306

stops.name: Eboracum, the acclamation over a dead father
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Constantius dies in the fortress at Eboracum on the twenty-fifth of July. Before the body is cold the troops put the purple on his son, and the sources name the man who pushes it forward: Crocus, king of the Alamanni, serving Rome with his own warband. It is an army's decision and not a college's. Galerius, presented with the fact, recognizes Constantine as caesar rather than as augustus, which is a refusal dressed as a concession. The system built to end dynastic succession has produced one in its first handover.
suggested_refs: The principia of the Sixth Legion beneath York Minster, and Philip Jackson's 1998 bronze of Constantine on the grass above it

stops.name: Trier, the Frankish kings and the wedding
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Frankish invasion falls in the winter of 306 to 307, and the executions and the marriage both belong to 307
stops.campa: The Franks cross the Rhine in the winter and Constantine breaks them. He takes their kings, Ascaric and Merogais, back to Trier and has them thrown to the beasts in the amphitheatre in front of the assembled city, and the panegyrist praises him for it at length. The same year, in the same city, he marries Fausta, daughter of Maximian. The old augustus has come out of retirement and needs a son-in-law with an army; Constantine needs a claim that is not simply a legion's shout in Britain. Both get what they came for.
suggested_refs: The Trier amphitheatre, and the Aula Palatina raised as Constantine's basilica in the same city

segments.name: Gaul, and the Road into Italy

stops.name: Massalia, the end of Maximian
stops.date_confidence: attested for the revolt and the death in 310; the manner of death is reported as suicide by sources written for the winning side
stops.campa: Maximian rebels a second time, now against the son-in-law he made, seizes the treasury at Arles and shuts himself inside Massalia. Constantine comes down the Rhone faster than anyone expects and the townspeople open the gates from within. Maximian is taken, spared in form, and shortly afterward hangs himself, which is what Lactantius says. The father-in-law who supplied the legitimacy is now a corpse that has to be explained. Constantine explains it by finding himself a better ancestor.
suggested_refs: The damnatio memoriae of Maximian across the western provinces after July 310

stops.name: Trier, the vision of Apollo
stops.date_confidence: attested as a speech, undatable as an experience: the panegyric of 25 July 310 reports the vision, and the anniversary it celebrates is his fifth year, not his tenth
stops.campa: An orator stands up at Trier for the fifth anniversary of the reign and announces a new lineage: Constantine descends from Claudius Gothicus, and Maximian is nobody. Then he tells the court that the emperor, turning aside to a temple in Gaul, saw Apollo himself with Victory, holding out laurel crowns marked with the number of years he would rule. It is the first sign in the sky in Constantine's official story, and the god inside it is the sun. Two years later there will be another sign, and a different god will be given the credit.
suggested_refs: The solar coinage of Constantine, SOLI INVICTO COMITI, struck through and past the year 312

stops.name: Segusio, the burned gate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the campaign, approximate for the month: the invasion of Italy opens in the spring of 312
stops.campa: He crosses the Cottian Alps with something near forty thousand men, a quarter of what he could have raised and a fraction of what Maxentius holds Italy with. Segusio shuts its gates against him. He burns them, storms the walls, and then puts out the fire himself and forbids his soldiers the sack. The panegyrist reports the mercy as strategy, and it is exactly that: every walled town in the Po valley is being shown, in a single afternoon, what resistance costs and what surrender costs.
suggested_refs: The Arch of Augustus at Susa, still standing beside the gate Constantine fired

stops.name: Augusta Taurinorum, the armored cavalry broken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, approximate for the month
stops.campa: Maxentius sends out his clibanarii, horse and rider both cased in iron, the heaviest cavalry the Roman West can put in a field. Constantine lets them charge into a line that opens as they come, closes on their flanks, and clubs them down with iron-shod maces where a lance cannot reach. The survivors run for Turin and find the gates shut against them by the city's own people, who then open those gates to Constantine. He has been in Italy a few weeks and the towns are already choosing.
suggested_refs: The clibanarii of the Maxentian field army, the last heavy cavalry of the old western establishment

stops.name: Verona, the prefect killed in the field
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle and the death, approximate for the month
stops.campa: Verona sits inside a loop of the Adige with Ruricius Pompeianus, Maxentius's praetorian prefect, holding it and the whole northern army behind its walls. Constantine crosses upstream, invests the town, beats Ruricius when he breaks out for reinforcements, then beats him again when he comes back with them. Ruricius dies in the field. The panegyrist has Constantine fighting in the line himself and being pulled out of it by his officers. After Verona there is no army between him and Rome.
suggested_refs: The Adige loop and the Roman walls of Verona, held by the last Maxentian field command in the north

stops.name: Pons Milvius, the sign and the river
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle on 28 October 312; disputed for the sign, since Eusebius reports a daylight cross of light with a Greek legend and Lactantius reports a dream the night before with no sky-sign and no motto, and the Latin formula in hoc signo vinces appears in neither
stops.campa: Maxentius, who has sat out two sieges behind the Aurelian walls, comes out to fight with the Tiber at his back and a bridge of boats for a line of retreat. The sources disagree about what Constantine saw. Eusebius gives a cross of light above the noon sun, seen by the whole army, and Christ in a dream afterward. Lactantius gives only the dream, and an instruction to mark the shields. Both agree about the marks on the shields. By evening the boat bridge is broken, Maxentius is in the river, and his head is going into Rome on a spear.
stops.quote: He said that about noon, when the day was already beginning to decline, he saw with his own eyes the trophy of a cross of light in the heavens, above the sun, and bearing the inscription, Conquer by this.
stops.quote_source: Eusebius, Life of Constantine I.28, tr. Ernest Cushing Richardson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, vol. 1
suggested_refs: Ponte Milvio, still carrying traffic over the Tiber on the site of the boat bridge

stops.name: Rome, the statue with the standard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the statue and its inscription, approximate for the date it was set up
stops.campa: He enters Rome, disbands the praetorian guard that made Maxentius, and has a statue of himself set up holding a tall spear shaped into a cross. Eusebius records the inscription he orders cut beneath it. The word Christ does not appear in it. Neither does Jupiter. What the formula names is a salutary sign and a tyranny broken, and it can be read in opposite directions by a senator and by a bishop standing in front of the same bronze, which is the whole point of writing it that way.
stops.quote: by virtue of this salutary sign, which is the true test of valor, I have preserved and liberated your city from the yoke of tyranny
stops.quote_source: Inscription ordered by Constantine beneath his own statue at Rome, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine I.40, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The disbanding of the Praetorian Guard and the razing of the Castra Praetoria barracks, 312

stops.name: Mediolanum, the wedding and the agreement
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting and the marriage in February 313; disputed for the instrument, since no edict was issued at Milan and the surviving text is Licinius's rescript published at Nicomedia in June, which many historians hold makes the traditional label wrong
stops.campa: Constantine marries his half-sister Constantia to Licinius at Milan, and the two augusti settle a religious policy between them over the wedding. There is no Edict of Milan. What exists is what the two agree here and what Licinius then publishes at Nicomedia in June, a rescript to a provincial governor restoring confiscated property and granting every man the worship he chooses. The name the tradition attached to the document is wrong. The thing itself, a state that stops requiring one religion, is not.
stops.quote: Perceiving long ago that religious liberty ought not to be denied, but that it ought to be granted to the judgment and desire of each individual to perform his religious duties according to his own choice
stops.quote_source: The Milan agreement as promulgated by Licinius, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History X.5, tr. Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The Licinian rescript posted at Nicomedia, 13 June 313, the only surviving text of the Milan settlement

stops.name: Rome, the arch and the tenth year
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Senate dedicates a triumphal arch beside the Colosseum for his tenth year. Most of the sculpture on it is cut off older monuments, Trajan's and Hadrian's and Marcus Aurelius's, with the heads recarved as Constantine's: a hundred and fifty years of imperial faces reissued under one name. The inscription says he beat the tyrant by greatness of mind and by instigation of the divinity. Which divinity is not stated. The Senate is pagan and the emperor is something else, and the formula is built so that neither has to say which.
suggested_refs: The Colossus of Constantine in the western apse of the Basilica of Maxentius, and the marble head and hand now in the Capitoline courtyard

stops.name: Cibalae, the first war with Licinius
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle; the year is given as 316 in most reckonings and as 314 in others, and the two chronologies have not been reconciled
stops.campa: Three years after the wedding the two augusti are at war over the Balkans. Constantine catches Licinius at Cibalae in Pannonia, fights him from dawn into the night, and holds the field. Licinius withdraws east and gets terms: he keeps Thrace and the East, he gives up Pannonia and Moesia and Macedonia, and both men treat the peace as an interval. Constantine takes the palace at Sirmium on the Sava for a forward base and spends the following years on the Danube against Sarmatians and Goths, which is also how an army is kept in condition.
suggested_refs: The imperial palace complex at Sirmium, excavated under modern Sremska Mitrovica

stops.name: Serdica, my Rome and the day of the Sun
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Sunday law of 321, uncertain in day and in place of issue: the codices give both 3 March and 3 July and do not agree where he was; the remark about Serdica survives only in later Byzantine tradition and no contemporary source records it
stops.campa: He is fond of Serdica and the Byzantines will remember him saying so: my Rome, he calls a Balkan road town. From these years comes the law that closes the courts and the city workshops on the venerable day of the Sun and leaves the farmers alone, because sowing does not wait on legislation. It is the first Sunday in Roman law. It is also addressed to the sun by name, the god of the Trier vision, and any Christian reading it can hear his own sabbath inside it if he wants to.
suggested_refs: The rotunda of St George at Sofia, the Constantinian-era brick building at the heart of Serdica

stops.name: Thessalonica, the harbor and the fleet
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline by Zosimus for the shipbuilding and harbor works in the buildup to 324; the individual years are not separable
stops.campa: He dredges the harbor at Thessalonica and builds two hundred thirty-oared warships and two thousand transports in it, works his army up past a hundred thousand foot and ten thousand horse, and then crosses the Danube after Gothic raiders into territory that is legally Licinius's. Licinius protests the violation, which is the last piece Constantine needed. The palace and rotunda that Galerius built in this city, for the persecution's chief architect, now house the man who is about to reunite the empire under the persecuted religion.
suggested_refs: The Rotunda and palace of Galerius at Thessalonica, reused as Constantine's forward base

stops.name: Hadrianopolis, the crossing of the Hebrus
stops.date_confidence: attested for 3 July 324, and distinct from Chrysopolis in September; older accounts that fold the two battles into one date are wrong
stops.campa: Licinius holds the far bank of the Hebrus outside Adrianople with the larger army. Constantine sends a visible detachment upstream to make a show of building a bridge, moves the real crossing to a wooded point with a ford, takes five thousand archers and the cavalry over, and is on the flank before the line can turn. The rout is complete. Licinius leaves his dead on the Hebrus and gets inside Byzantium with what he can save, and from here the war moves onto water.
suggested_refs: The Hebrus, modern Maritsa, and the field outside Adrianople where the western army crossed

stops.name: The Hellespont, Crispus in the narrows
stops.date_confidence: attested by Zosimus for the campaign of 324; the exact days are not recorded
stops.campa: Crispus, Constantine's eldest son by Minervina, takes eighty ships into the narrows against a fleet of three hundred and fifty that cannot deploy in a channel that width. Zosimus names the enemy admiral Abantus; the form Amandus reaches some later accounts, and the two have never been reconciled. The fleet is wrecked over two days, half of it by a gale off the Asian shore. The straits open, the transports come through, and Licinius abandons Byzantium and crosses to Chalcedon.
suggested_refs: The Dardanelles narrows, where the numbers of the eastern fleet counted against it

stops.name: Chrysopolis, sole ruler of the Roman world
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Licinius has raised a fresh army on the Asian side and put Martinian into the purple beside him. Constantine ferries across from Byzantium, which he has been besieging all summer with mounds and towers, and destroys them at Chrysopolis on the eighteenth of September. Licinius runs to Nicomedia and Constantia goes to her brother to beg for her husband's life. He is spared, sent to Thessalonica, and killed there the next year anyway. Constantine is fifty-two, there is no other emperor anywhere, and within weeks he is legislating to the eastern provinces about the God who handed him the field.
stops.quote: To all who entertain just and sound sentiments respecting the character of the Supreme Being, it has long been most clearly evident
stops.quote_source: Constantine, Law Respecting the Christian Religion, addressed to the provincials of Palestine, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine II.24, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: Chrysopolis, modern Uskudar, on the Asian shore opposite the city Constantine is about to found

segments.name: New Rome, Nicaea, and the Killings of 326

stops.name: Byzantium, the furrow traced with a spear
stops.date_confidence: attested for the foundation rites of November 324; the walking legend is preserved by Philostorgius and by later chroniclers, not by a contemporary
stops.campa: Six weeks after Chrysopolis he begins the city. He walks the line of the new walls himself with a spear point dragging in the ground, out past anything Byzantium has ever enclosed, and when his attendants ask how much further he means to go he answers: until the one who walks ahead of me stops. He is fixing the seam between Europe and Asia as a street address. Fifteen centuries later Napoleon, stalled in front of Acre, will say he would have returned to Paris by way of Constantinople, and mean this ground.
suggested_refs: The line of the Constantinian land wall, superseded within a century by the walls of Theodosius II

stops.name: Nicaea, the council on the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested for the opening in May 325; the close is disputed, given variously as 19 June for the subscription of the creed, as the first weeks of July, and as 25 August
stops.campa: He summons the bishops of the whole world to a lakeside palace in Bithynia at public expense, men who were in the mines twenty years ago under Diocletian, and opens the session himself in purple. The question is whether the Son is of the same substance as the Father. He does not decide it; he presides over its being decided and then puts the state behind the answer. Arius is condemned and exiled. The creed goes out. The council closes into the festival of his twentieth year on the throne.
stops.quote: I pray therefore that no malignant adversary may henceforth interfere to mar our happy state
stops.quote_source: Constantine's opening address to the Council of Nicaea, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.12, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The Nicene Creed of 325, and the lakeside palace at Iznik whose foundations lie under the water

stops.name: Pola, the death of Crispus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the month: the year 326 and the place Pola are attested, no ancient source gives a month, and modern reconstructions put the death around May on the road to Rome
stops.campa: Crispus, caesar for nearly nine years, victor of the Hellespont, the son named on the coinage, is arrested and put to death at Pola in Istria, apparently without a trial. No source supplies a charge that the other sources accept. His name is chiselled off inscriptions across the empire. Constantine never issues an explanation, and Eusebius, writing the life eleven years afterward, writes as though Crispus had never existed. Whatever happened at Pola, the record of it was destroyed deliberately and the destruction worked.
suggested_refs: The erased inscriptions of Crispus, the fullest damnatio memoriae of the Constantinian house

stops.name: Rome, the Capitol not climbed
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was in Rome in July 326 for the close of his twentieth year, and not his thirtieth as some accounts have it; disputed for the refusal itself, which is reported only by the hostile Zosimus
stops.campa: He comes to Rome in July for the twentieth anniversary and the city expects the old circuit: the procession up the hill, the sacrifice to Jupiter Optimus Maximus at the top of it. Zosimus says he refuses to climb, insults the rite in front of the Senate, and loses the city for good. Zosimus is a pagan writing a century and a half later with a case to argue, and no other source confirms him. What is certain is the negative: Constantine never enters Rome again in the eleven years he has left.
suggested_refs: The Capitoline temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, terminus of the triumphal route Constantine did not walk

stops.name: Rome, the death of Fausta
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year is traditional and the Roman setting defensible, but the whole episode rests on hostile or much later sources, the overheated bath is later still, and Eusebius omits the death entirely
stops.campa: Fausta, augusta, mother of three future emperors, daughter and sister and wife of emperors, dies within months of her stepson. The story that reaches the Middle Ages has her accusing Crispus of assaulting her, and Helena afterward telling her son the truth, and Fausta shut into a steam bath until she suffocates. Zosimus supplies the frame and the bath is a later addition. Her name comes off the inscriptions too. A dynasty that will hold the empire for another thirty-seven years is founded on one summer's silence.
suggested_refs: The silence of Eusebius, who narrates the reign at length and never mentions either death

stops.name: Jerusalem, the ground under the temple of Venus
stops.date_confidence: attested for the commission and the excavation; the year of Helena's arrival is given as 326 or as 327, and the finding of the wood of the cross is a later tradition that Eusebius, who reports the dig, does not mention
stops.campa: He orders the temple of Venus on the hill in Aelia Capitolina pulled down and its fill carted out of the city, and beneath it, Eusebius says, the tomb comes up out of the ground against all expectation. Macarius the bishop receives an imperial letter and an open order on the provincial treasuries: columns, marble, gold for the ceiling, whatever the work needs. Helena is in Palestine in these years, old, spending the treasury on churches. The discovery of the true cross is told later, by other people.
stops.quote: Forasmuch as the unholy and willful rule of tyranny has persecuted the servants of our Saviour until this present time
stops.quote_source: Constantine, letter on the building of churches, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine II.46, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The rock-cut tomb inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Hadrianic fill that preserved it

stops.name: Bethlehem, the cave and the octagon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the foundations; the dates are approximate, running roughly from 327 to 333, and Eusebius credits Helena while the funding is imperial
stops.campa: Helena raises a basilica over the cave at Bethlehem where the birth is placed, and a third church on the Mount of Olives at the cave of the teaching before the Ascension. Eusebius makes the pair of them monuments to two mysteries and to an old woman travelling the provinces with imperial authority and no office. The octagon at Bethlehem is cut so that a pilgrim can look down through the floor into the rock. It is the only one of the three churches that has never been destroyed.
suggested_refs: The Eleona basilica on the Mount of Olives, third of the Constantinian foundations in Palestine

stops.name: Nicomedia, the oration to the assembly of the saints
stops.date_confidence: attested as a text transmitted with Eusebius, unfixed in occasion: the venue is proposed as Serdica, Thessalonica, Nicomedia, Antioch or Rome, and the year anywhere from 317 to 328; the pin here follows one defensible reading and is not a settled one
stops.campa: On a Good Friday the emperor preaches. He argues from the Hebrew prophets, then from the Erythraean Sibyl, and then he reads out the fourth eclogue of Virgil, the poem about a child whose birth turns the age of iron back into gold, and tells the assembly it is a prophecy of Christ written forty years before the birth. That reading is the reason the church keeps Virgil. It is the reason Dante, a thousand years later, is handed a pagan for a guide through hell and does not have to justify the choice.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Oration to the Assembly of the Saints'
suggested_refs: Virgil's fourth eclogue and its Christian reception, from this reading forward to Dante's Inferno

stops.name: Drepanum, the village renamed for his mother
stops.date_confidence: attested for the refounding and the new name; the year is approximate, and Helena's birth there is tradition rather than record, her birthplace being claimed also by Naissus, Edessa and Trier
stops.campa: He rebuilds a fishing village on the gulf of Nicomedia, gives it city rights and tax relief, and names it Helenopolis, because the martyr Lucian is buried there and because Helena is said to have been born there. The saying is not certain and three other towns claim her. The gesture is what is certain: a woman set aside as a wife thirty-five years earlier, of a family nobody troubled to record, now has an imperial city on the map carrying her name and coins struck with her face.
suggested_refs: The site of Helenopolis at Hersek in Altinova, on the gulf of Izmit

stops.name: Rome, Helena on the Via Labicana
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial in the rotunda on the Via Labicana; the death is dated between about 328 and 330 and the year is not fixed, and the porphyry sarcophagus may have been cut for Constantine himself
stops.campa: Helena dies at about eighty with her son present, Eusebius says, and is carried to Rome and laid in a rotunda on the Via Labicana beside the barracks of the mounted guard. Her sarcophagus is porphyry, the imperial stone, carved with cavalry and captured barbarians: battle scenes for a woman who never saw a battle, and the guess is that it was cut for Constantine and handed to her instead. He will not be buried in Rome. He has a better city by now and it is not finished yet.
suggested_refs: The porphyry sarcophagus of Helena in the Vatican Museums, and the ruined rotunda at Tor Pignattara

stops.name: Constantinople, the dedication of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eleventh of May the city is dedicated with forty days of ceremony, chariot races, a distribution of bread, and a gilded statue of Fortune carried into the hippodrome. It has a senate, a free grain dole taken off Egypt, churches, and no old temples worth the name. Two centuries on, the bones of Saint Barbara will be brought here from Heliopolis, because this is where relics are understood to belong. He calls it New Rome. Everyone else calls it after him, and always will.
suggested_refs: The Tyche of Constantinople, the city's Fortune, carried in procession at every anniversary of the dedication

stops.name: Constantinople, the porphyry column
stops.date_confidence: attested for the column and its dedication in 330, with erection begun around 328; the reported contents of the base and the earlier identity of the bronze statue come from later and unreliable sources
stops.campa: In the oval forum they raise a shaft of porphyry drums near fifty meters high with a bronze Constantine on top: radiate crown, spear, orb, the emperor as Helios, the sun god of the Trier vision standing over a Christian capital. In 1179 a knight out of Lorraine, Pierre de Bourlemont, will sail into the Golden Horn and crane up at the porphyry emperors. A gale takes the statue down in 1106, crusaders strip the bronze wreaths in 1204, and Ottoman iron hoops bind the burnt shaft into what Istanbul calls the hooped stone.
suggested_refs: The Cemberlitas column, 34.8 meters of scorched porphyry still standing on the Divan Yolu

stops.name: Constantinople, the thirtieth year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the tricennalia celebrations of 335 and 336 are not documented in the fetched sources with the detail the anniversary would warrant, and the remark to the bishops is preserved by Eusebius without a date or a place
stops.campa: The thirtieth year of the reign, longer than any emperor since Augustus. Eusebius comes to the capital and delivers a panegyric on him. At a dinner for bishops somewhere in these years Constantine says the sentence that will be quoted in every argument about church and state for the next fifteen centuries, and the bishops, Eusebius reports, applaud it. He is unbaptized. He has convened an ecumenical council, exiled a heresiarch and then recalled him, and never once received communion.
stops.quote: You are bishops whose jurisdiction is within the Church: I also am a bishop, ordained by God to overlook whatever is external to the Church.
stops.quote_source: Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.24, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1); the remark is undated in the source
suggested_refs: Eusebius's tricennalian oration, delivered before the emperor in Constantinople

stops.name: Constantinople, the letters to the desert
stops.date_confidence: attested by Athanasius for the correspondence; the year is approximate, the letters themselves do not survive, and the reply is transmitted only in the Life of Antony
stops.campa: The emperor and his sons Constantius and Constans write to an illiterate Copt in the Egyptian desert, addressing him as father and asking for an answer. Antony wants to throw the letters away and says he does not know how a man replies to an emperor. His monks tell him the emperors are Christians and would be wounded, so he dictates one back: he urges them not to think much of the present, to remember the judgment coming, and to know that Christ alone is the true and everlasting king.
suggested_refs: Athanasius's Life of Antony, chapter 81, on the imperial letters and the monk's reply

stops.name: Achyron, the springs and the last villa
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Eusebius reports the illness and the withdrawal in the spring of 337, and the exact site of Achyron has never been securely identified
stops.campa: He means to be baptized in the Jordan and he has been putting it off for thirty years, on the reasoning that baptism washes everything away and is therefore best taken last. In the spring he falls ill, leaves the city for the hot baths near Helenopolis, prays at the shrine of the martyr Lucian there, and is carried on to a suburban villa near Nicomedia called Achyron. He is in the middle of preparing a Persian campaign. He summons the bishops there and tells them the delay is over.
stops.quote: The time is arrived which I have long hoped for, with an earnest desire and prayer that I might obtain the salvation of God
stops.quote_source: Constantine to the assembled bishops at Achyron, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.62, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The hot springs at Pythia Therma near Helenopolis, the emperor's last cure

stops.name: Nicomedia, the white robe
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death on 22 May 337 and for the deathbed baptism; the baptizer is Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian, and later tradition worked hard to substitute a Roman baptism by Sylvester instead
stops.campa: He calls the bishops in and asks for it, and Eusebius of Nicomedia baptizes him, and afterward he puts on the white robe of the newly baptized and will not touch the purple again. He dies on Pentecost, the twenty-second of May. The man who baptizes the first Christian emperor belongs to the party that emperor's own council condemned twelve years before at Nicaea, and no ancient source friendly to Constantine finds this comfortable to report. The West will eventually invent a different baptism to replace it.
stops.quote: Now I know that I am truly blessed: now I feel assured that I am accounted worthy of immortality, and am made a partaker of Divine light.
stops.quote_source: Constantine after receiving baptism, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.63, tr. Richardson (NPNF II.1)
suggested_refs: The legend of Constantine's baptism by Pope Sylvester at Rome, the counter-tradition built to erase the Arian bishop

stops.name: Constantinople, among the Twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial in the mausoleum at the Holy Apostles; the church was unfinished at his death and completed by Constantius II, and the month of the interment is not fixed
stops.campa: The body goes back to the city in a gold coffin, lies in state in the palace with the officers doing obeisance to an empty throne, and is buried in the mausoleum attached to the Church of the Holy Apostles at the high point of his city. He has set twelve memorials in it, one for each apostle, with his own sarcophagus in the middle of them. Constantius II finishes the church his father did not. The empire is split between three sons within four months, and they open their reigns by killing their uncles.
suggested_refs: The Constantinian mausoleum at the Holy Apostles, the model for every imperial burial church that follows

stops.name: Reims, the new Constantine at the font
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the baptism as the tradition records it, with the year disputed between 496, 498 and 508, and Gregory of Tours writing eighty years afterward
stops.campa: A Frankish king vows to Clotilde's God in the middle of a battle at Tolbiac when his line is breaking, and wins, and comes to Reims at Christmas to be baptized by Remigius. The chroniclers call Clovis a new Constantine as he goes down to the font, and they mean the Milvian Bridge precisely: the god called on in extremity who delivers the field that day. Constantine has been dead a hundred and sixty years and is already a mold that other kings can be poured into. Every Christian monarchy in the West will use it.
suggested_refs: The baptistery site under Reims cathedral, and the phrase novus Constantinus in the Frankish chronicles

stops.name: Rome, the letter he never wrote
stops.date_confidence: attested that Leo IX cites the document in 1054; the document is a forgery of roughly the eighth century and the date and circumstances of its composition are not fixed
stops.campa: A document surfaces in which Constantine, cured of leprosy by Pope Sylvester, hands the pope the Lateran, the city of Rome, Italy and the western provinces, and withdraws east so as not to crowd him. Leo IX cites it in 1054 in the quarrel that splits the churches. Charlemagne is crowned inside its logic, and Otto III chooses a pope who takes the name Sylvester on purpose. For seven centuries the strongest claim the papacy holds over kings is a letter an emperor never dictated.
suggested_refs: The Constitutum Constantini, and the Sylvester cycle frescoed at Santi Quattro Coronati in Rome

stops.name: Naples, the word fief
stops.date_confidence: attested for the treatise of 1439 to 1440, written at the Aragonese court at Naples; it circulates in manuscript and is not printed until 1506
stops.campa: Lorenzo Valla, in the pay of Alfonso of Aragon and useful to him precisely because Alfonso is quarreling with the pope, takes the Donation apart on its Latin. The document uses words the fourth century did not have. It says fief. It describes a Constantinople that does not exist yet at the date it claims for itself. Valla proves the strongest charter in Europe is a forgery using nothing but grammar, and the method he builds here is what philology will afterward do to every sacred text it touches.
sources: Lorenzo Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione (1439-1440)
suggested_refs: Valla's Declamatio, printed 1506 and taken up by Ulrich von Hutten and the Reformation polemicists

stops.name: Fatih, the mosque over the mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: attested for the demolition around 1461 and the mosque built between 1463 and 1470; the patriarchate had already moved out to the Pammakaristos in 1456, before the church came down, and the order of events is often reported backwards
stops.campa: Crusaders opened the imperial tombs here for the gold in 1204. After 1453 the Holy Apostles stands empty and rotting, the patriarch moves his seat to another church, and Mehmed II has the building pulled down and raises his own mosque on the highest hill of the city. Nothing of the tomb is above ground. Marco Polo's father set out from this city and Ibn Battuta was received at its court, and both walked past a mausoleum that no longer exists; a fragment of porphyry in a museum case is the whole physical remainder.
suggested_refs: The imperial porphyry sarcophagi from the Holy Apostles, displayed in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums

stops.name: York, the bronze on the grass
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Outside the south transept of York Minster, over the buried headquarters of the Sixth Legion, a bronze Constantine sits with a broken sword across his knees, put there by Philip Jackson in 1998. The plinth reads: Constantine by this sign conquer. He was proclaimed roughly under where that pavement now lies, by soldiers, on the strength of his father's body and an Alamannic king's opinion. Seventeen centuries of Christendom rest on a fortnight's decision taken in a British garrison town.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of Constantine the Great, York'
suggested_refs: The Roman principia under York Minster, excavated beneath the cathedral's central tower
